I call to order the informal meeting of the plenary on the UNAT initiative. I would like to welcome you all here. This is the seventh in our series of monthly briefings intended to keep the membership informed and to sustain the momentum as the UNAT initiative advances. Today, we will hear an overall update on the UNAT initiative from Under-Secretary-General Guy Ryder, followed by briefings on two work packages, work package 22, prevention, peacebuilding, peace support, and work package 18 and 21 on funding mechanisms and systems-wide results management. I give the floor to Mr. Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy. The floor is yours, sir.

Thank you very much, Chair. Good morning to everybody. Chair, Excellencies, thank you for joining us for today's briefing on the UN80 initiative. Through you, Chair, thanks to the PGA for once again providing us with this opportunity and for her very steadfast commitment to advance the initiative. I want to take the chance to reflect briefly on progress overall since our last briefing and then turn to the work that lies ahead of us. In June, I underlined the importance, in particular, of the ECOSOC resolution then under negotiation on the quadriennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the UN system. Today, I am pleased to note that ECOSOC adopted the resolution by consensus last week. In our view, it reaffirms the direction of travel for reconfiguring country teams around what countries really need, deploying expertise where it is required, expanding shared back office services, following up on the funding compact and recalibrating the resident coordinator system. Member States also requested further information on financing, governance and country-level implications, amongst other things. These are central implementation questions on which the Secretary-General will revert to you with concrete responses through the established processes. On workstream two, that's the one on mandates, the General Assembly resolution on strengthening ECOSOC adopted last Friday requested ECOSOC to apply the outcomes of the mandate implementation review consistently through its own decision-making processes. And I think that this is welcome recognition and application of the progress made under this work stream of UNAT and of ECOSOC's role in carrying it forward. So let me thank the permanent representatives of Barbados and Malta and Switzerland for facilitating those resolutions. Together, we are adapting the UN system to deliver better, based on a strong shared foundation. Other elements have advanced as well. We published the unified services roadmap alongside a feasibility study on global shared services on 1 July. It provides, for the first time, shared evidence and a joint approach to common operational services across pillars and at both the global and the country levels. Member States can support the roadmap in the relevant governing bodies. And if that is done, cost savings of 20 to 80% for key back office services will become possible. Internally, the executive office of the Secretary General through the Schefter Cabinet has also issued new reporting guidance this month. Reports will become clearer, more focused, and we hope accordingly more useful for member states. Work has also continued in our support to member states efforts in the ad hoc working group on the mandate implementation review. And here I think one lesson stands out very clearly. and that is that effective review depends on accessible information on how specific resolutions and decisions are implemented, and we'll be reverting to that question in our examination of specific work packages today. Now looking forward, between now and September, Member States can expect further important developments in three areas of work. Firstly, We will continue to share information briefs, reports and other products as work packages within the Secretary General's authority progress. Implementation will also continue where authority already rests with the Secretary General, including on the mechanics of expertise on demand, on technology acceleration and on the data commons into ALIA. Secondly, Proposals requiring intergovernmental consideration will proceed through the appropriate processes which have been set out, whether in this session, the 81st session, or the governing bodies of relevant entities. The immediate proposal requiring Member State consideration during this session is the Secretary-General's report on the proposed merger of the United Nations System Staff College and UNITAR. It is a clear articulation of how we can deliver better if we join forces, platforms and services where this makes sense. Thirdly, we will continue supporting the work of the ad hoc working group by making relevant information more readily accessible to member states. And this includes enhancing the mandate registry so you can navigate from each resolution to its implementation as seen in reports and other materials and to the funding and results of the programs that make reference to them. Our purpose is to make implementation easier to understand and review and to needless to say, authority over mandates remains with you, our member states. Our aim in all of this work, of course, is enable you to be more effective stewards of these mandates. Underpinning all of this work is our shared responsibility to move the organization forward for the benefit of the people that it serves. And in that regard, Let me draw attention to the fact that on the 9th of July, the Secretary General joined 500 civil society representatives in person and hundreds more online for an open dialogue on the United Nations of the future. The civil society representatives voiced strong support for a more inclusive, effective and responsive United Nations, and they engaged constructively on how the work under the UNAT initiative can help shape precisely that. Their message was, I think, quite straightforward but compelling. Renewal must be shaped with people and not only for them. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the work packages that we will discuss today, and Chair, you've already outlined what they are, take that proposition from principle to practice. They examine how we bring together dispersed capacities so that they serve people better, how we design funding so that it serves mandates better, and how we connect mandates and resources more clearly to results to demonstrate the difference that we all want to make together. So in conclusion, I think that UNAT is now becoming a test, not of our willingness to discuss reform, but of our ability to deliver on it. The next phase therefore belongs to all of us, and we look forward to your guidance and to turning that guidance into action. And I thank you for your attention.
I thank the Under-Secretary-General for Policy. I give the floor to Ms. Elizabeth Spehar, Assistant Secretary-General for Peacebuilding and Peace Support.

Thank you very much, Chair, and thanks to all of you Member States who have come this morning in great numbers for this session. I'm really honored to have been asked to brief you this morning on work package 22 on prevention, peacebuilding and peace support, and in particular on what is identified as action 55, aligned surge capacity for peace and security. rule of law, disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration, security sector reform, small arms control, mission transitions, prevention of extremist violence and counter terrorism to support regional needs. I will refer to the work that is being conducted in two parts, one longer than the other. The first part is the establishment of the peacebuilding and peace support office, which speaks precisely to the imperative of trying to bring our tools more coherently together in support of prevention, peacebuilding and peace support. Secondly, there is a mapping exercise that is intended precisely to capture the information on what surge capacity exists in the system in the areas that I just mentioned a moment ago. First of all, on the first part, I wanted to start by underscoring, as we all know, that peace and security, including conflict prevention and sustaining peace, have been central to the purpose of the UN since its inception, and in the evolving global context marked by multipolarity, fragmentation and surging violent conflict, they are more urgent than ever. we have some very strong messages and commitments and decisions from member states through the pact for the future the two thousand and twenty five review of the un peacebuilding architecture and its unanimous twin general assembly and security council resolutions all affirming a shared commitment to nationally led prevention and peacebuilding efforts and to having a more comprehensive approach to building and sustaining peace. We also, of course, have the guidance of the new agenda for peace of the Secretary General that came out in the middle of 2023. In the Pact for the Future, member states also requested the Secretary General to undertake a review of the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations. I've heard many Member States express the hope that that particular review, which I understand will be coming out very soon, and the outcome of last year's peacebuilding architecture review will somehow speak to each other. Indeed, the Secretary General expresses, I would say, the same sentiments in his report, Shifting Paradigms, United to Deliver, which was an update report on the UNAD initiatives, where he acknowledged that peace and security work has been split across mandates, offices and missions, often disconnected from the rest of the system. The report commits that, and here I quote the Secretary General, the peace and security pillar will emphasize prevention, peacebuilding and political solutions. It will adapt its systems and architecture to be lean, agile and field focused, delivering impact across mission and non-mission settings, end of quotation. We are also in the process through this new office of working to bring peacebuilding and rule of law efforts closer together. This also aligns with the Secretary-General's vision of the rule of law itself as, and here I quote him from his new vision for the rule of law of 2023, rule of law being the foundation for conflict prevention, peacemaking, peacekeeping, sustaining peace, and peacebuilding, end of quote. So in response to these imperatives and the call of yourselves, the member states, One of the first outputs of the UN80 initiative focusing on structural reforms has been the establishment of the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office, or PBPSO, in DPPA-DPO. So it spans both the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the Department of Peace Operations. The creation of this office was intended to bring together tools, expertise, financing, and partnerships so that support to member states and partners is more integrated on prevention, peacebuilding, and sustaining peace. The goal, indeed, is to make the UN's prevention, peacebuilding, and peace support capacities easier to identify, coordinate, and deploy to missions as well as in non-mission settings as appropriate and in support of nationally led priorities. The office was established in January 2026. It comprises the former peacebuilding support office, which includes the management of the secretary general's peacebuilding fund. It serves as a secretariat for the intergovernmental peacebuilding commission, and it has quite robust programmatic and partnership assistance. And this new office has brought together those three areas together with three components of the former Office of the Rule of Law and Security Institutions of the Department of Peace Operations, namely the Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration Unit, DDRU, the Justice and Corrections Service, JCS, and the Security Sector Reform Unit, SSRU, which now together form the core of PBPSO's integrated support to member states, partners, and the UN system. And I would recall that in his, again, in his shifting paradigms report, PBPSO was envisaged by the Secretary General as a quote, center of excellence on prevention, peacebuilding and peace support, unquote. So as I mentioned a moment ago, the office was formally set up in the middle of January 2026 following member state approval. and since then has been working to consolidate and enhance a more coherent and effective offer, as we call it, in the area of peacebuilding and peace support in mission and non-mission contexts, and to do so more effectively and in a more integrated manner, aiming to become, as I often say to my interlocutors, greater than the sum of its six parts, and working closely with other parts of the UN and other partners to this end. I wanted to underscore an important role within the system that we can contribute to as PBPSO. In addition to its own tools and capacities that I have very briefly mentioned, PBPSO has tools to enhance a bridging and hinge role across the system. What I mean by that is that PBPSO can serve as a very useful bridge between the work of the peace and security pillar and the prevention peacebuilding work of the broader system through the agency's funds and programs. We are part of the peace and security pillar, but we also work very closely with the agency's funds and programs across the board, given the comprehensive nature of peacebuilding and sustaining peace. It also plays a hinge role, as the Secretary-General has mentioned in many of his reports on peacebuilding and sustaining peace by working across pillars and trying to bring together the humanitarian, development and peace elements of the system to work more coherently together in service of member states for building and sustaining peace over time. The PBPSO does this in various ways, including through specialized coordination networks, and I'll name some of them. We co-lead with UNDP some of these. We have the interagency working group on DDR, the interagency SSR task force, the global focal point for rule of law, interagency task force on transitional justice, and the UN system-wide peacebuilding contact and strategy groups. So these are some of the mechanisms we have as an office to really try to contribute to a more integrated, UN when it comes to peacebuilding, peace support and sustaining peace. The office has identified in these early months of its existence four core areas where we believe we could add particular value as a cohesive support entity, working of course very closely alongside other actors, including alongside many of our UN partners. In addition to UN mission settings, of course, I think we can have a particularly useful role in settings of mission transitions, UN mission transitions, the area of institution building for sustaining peace, support for nationally owned and led prevention and peacebuilding strategies, and in the area of peace finance. I can elaborate on some of those areas if you wish in the question and answer period. I'd like to if time permits, I will give you a couple of examples of the integrated approach that we hope to continue to support going forward with two country examples. One is the example of Sao Tome and Principe, where PBPSO has played quite a useful role. First of all, as secretariat to the intergovernmental peacebuilding commission, to which Sao Tome and Principe went to talk about its peacebuilding priorities and to get accompaniment and support. We were able, upon the request of the government, to provide some very critical support in the area of more equitable access to justice and security sector reform through a peacebuilding fund project. We were also able to put forward important tools that we have now in PBPSO in the area of support to security sector governance and reform and rule of law tools in order to help the country, including with the production or the establishment of its first ever national, first ever comprehensive security sector review. and also its first ever national prevention strategy, which it presented to the PBC last year. Another example is in the Central African Republic, where the Office, working in close coordination with UN field presences, has been instrumental in advancing transitional justice and the fight against impunity. This again was in relation to the role of the Peacebuilding Commission, which we backstop as secretariat. The PBC helped sustain political support for key peacebuilding priorities, including transitional justice, and aligned with MINUSCA's mandate through the global focal point arrangement and our own PP/PSO standing capacities. We were able to support collaboration between MINUSCA, UNDP, and other partners to strengthen the Special Criminal Court, while Peacebuilding Fund financing has been critical in supporting the Truth, Justice, Reparation, and Reconciliation Commission and the complementarity between that commission and the Special Criminal Court. To finish on the issue of the new office, I should say that the establishment and now the consolidation of this new office remains a work in progress. It is only about six months into this process. into this new configuration. I really hope to have more opportunities to engage with Member States on the new office, perhaps in smaller groups, because I feel that we are in a very important moment of co-creation and clearly because this office, as all of the Secretariat, is in service of Member States' needs, it would be very important to hear from you and to co-create. And finally, In support of the comprehensive overview, that's the second part of this work package that I wanted to underscore, in support of the comprehensive overview called for under work package 22, action 55, which I described a moment ago, PBPSO is coordinating a mapping to capture the capacities within the secretariat that provide surge support to the UN and member states in the areas of peace and security. broadly, but in particular rule of law as well, disarmament, demobilization and reintegration, security sector reform, small arms control, mission transitions, prevention of extremist violence and counter-terrorism from across DPO and DPPA in addition to the Office of Disarmament Affairs and the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism. We've already had several meetings with our colleagues on this issue. As we know, these capacities play a crucial role both in mission and non-mission settings. And the mapping, I think, will be particularly useful. I'm hoping it will be also, again, utilized in conjunction with the work that's being done on expertise on demand, which is another part of the UNAD process, mapping capacities writ large across the system that are available to member states. But this particular mapping will provide information about existing capacities, their offer, profiles, location, funding arrangements, deployment, notice period, and contacts, ensuring that the information is fully accessible and well connected to complementary UN work streams, such as the one I just mentioned, expertise on demand, also regional reset, and several others. And we hope to share the results of this mapping exercise by September. Thank you very much.

I thank the Assistant Secretary General for Peacebuilding and Peace Support. I give the floor now to Mr. James Wondal, Special Advisor to the Secretary General on Reforms, who will be joining us online. The floor is yours, sir.

Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, let me begin with the common thread that connects the two work packages I will present today. The United Nations has been entrusted by member states with thousands of mandates. They range from very specific tasks to the implementation of complex conventions. global frameworks and agendas such as the Sustainable Development Goals. Delivering these mandates require United Nations that can work across organizational boundaries, bring together different capabilities and adapt its presence and response to very different contexts. And ultimately, delivery happens somewhere. It happens globally, it happens regionally, but above all, it happens country by country. responding to national needs and in the development system to the priorities agreed with governments through the cooperation framework. And that brings us to a very simple question. Can we draw a clear line from the mandates member states give us as the United Nations to the resources we use and to the results we achieve? Today, that line is often difficult to see. The two work packages address this challenge from two connected directions. The work package 21 is about managing for results, and work package 18 is about financing for results. So let me make the following points. We need a clear system-wide line of sight from mandates to results. The UN has many strong results systems, Funds, programmes, specialised agencies and secretariat entities plan, monitor and report extensively. The gap is at the system level. We still lack a sufficiently credible and consistent way to connect mandate, resources and results. I think that matters for Member States. You receive a great deal of reporting, but it can still be difficult to see the collective picture. what the United Nations as a system is trying to achieve, what resources and capabilities are being applied, and where the constraints are and what collective results are being achieved. It also matters for the UN leadership because managing a system requires the ability to see across institutional boundaries. Work package 21 therefore proposes a system-wide management for results mechanism. And the idea is, you can say deliberately practical and it's also a light touch. As its center would be a structured management process through which the Secretary General and the UN principles can periodically look across the system, identify the small number of results that matter most for collective performance, understand constraints and adjust where needed. This requires common norms and standards that allow us progressively to connect mandates, resources and results across organizations without replacing the management and accountability system of individual entities. It is a mechanism for better collective management of the United Nations. And here, Member State dialogue is an integral part of that mechanism. Because management for results requires a structured dialogue between UN leadership and member states. That dialogue should be strategic, focused and facts-based. What results are we collectively seeking? What is working? Where are the constraints? Where do priorities and capabilities need to adjust? This creates an opportunity for continuing political conversation about mandate delivery, rather than relying primarily on a succession of individual reports. And importantly, we envisage developing this through consultations with member states. The coming period therefore includes consultations, development of system-wide results standards and norms, and ultimately piloting, you can say, an executive results dialogue before a full mechanism is proposed or even finalized. Now that brings me directly to work package 18, which is about funding. Once we ask what results the system is expected to deliver, we also have to ask how those results are financed. The funding review starts from the financing reality we expect to face. Resources are under pressure, core funding is constrained, earmarked funding accounts for the large majority of voluntary resources, and is likely to continue doing so. Pool funding has important strategic value, but remains comparatively small. So our proposition is to see the funding mix as a mix and see how we can get it to work better for mandate delivery. In other words, core, pooled and earmarked funding, they all have a role. They perform different functions. And we need to use each where it creates the greatest value and manage them increasingly as a coherent portfolio, or if you will, as a funding mix. Let me just go through them. Core funding provides the institutional foundation. It creates the capacity to maintain expertise, country presence, normative and policy capabilities, oversight, strategic planning. and their ability to respond when circumstances change. These capacities support the delivery of all forms of funding. The UN therefore has work to do in demonstrating what value core funding creates more clearly. And one of our recommendation is very practical. Entities should be able to explain simply and credibly what your core funding supports. Member States should be able to see the countries reached, the capabilities sustained, and the results that flexible resources make possible. Better results communication and greater transparency are essential to making the case for flexible funding of core. Let me now turn to pooled financing. Pool financing or pool funding allows member states to finance a collective UN response rather than a series of separate organizational interventions. That can be especially valuable where challenge cuts across mandates or sectors, or where a cooperation framework requires several UN entities to combine their capabilities around national priorities. We therefore propose stronger strategic positioning of pool funding updated guidance to capture recent positive innovations and a clearer portfolio perspective across the system. We also propose to repositioning the joint SDG fund as a Secretary General's fund for development, a principal instrument for catalytic development action alongside the established models providing by the Central Emergency Response Fund, the CERF and the Peacebuilding Fund that Elizabeth Speer heads. Let me turn to earmarking. Earmarking, we need to acknowledge that it has become central to the UN's financing model and will remain so. Its design though matters enormously. A large multi-year contribution allied with an agreed program or cooperation framework can provide substantial strategic value, a good quality earmarking. A small, short-term, highly customized project that requires separate agreements, reporting, and visibility arrangements and management processes sometimes create costs disproportionate to the resources provided. And we consider that a lower quality earmarking. We therefore propose a common framework for assessing the quality of earmarked funding. looking at alignment, duration, scale, flexibility and reporting requirements, risks and institutional costs. And we propose greater discipline on the UN side as well to understand the costing of low quality earmarking and increasingly face it out where possible. Let me now turn to the funding dialogue. Here, the idea is that the funding dialogue must become more strategic, particularly at the country level. This may be one of the most important practical implications for member states. At country level, we already have strategic framework, national priorities and the cooperation framework. But we need a funding dialogue that increasingly asks, are resources aligned with those priorities? What are the financing gaps? Where pooled financing create real value? And where is the earmarking that increased fragmentation? and what adjustments would allow the UN system to respond better to the country needs. We think that resident coordinators can help create that strategic space with governments, member states, and UN country teams and financing partners. At the global level, we similarly recommend a stronger funding compact dialogue through existing mechanisms, including a more strategic annual review within a suitable member state mechanism. And this is where the two packages, they come together. They come together around results. Because better financing depends on greater confidence. And greater confidence depends on transparency, accountability, and credible evidence of results. So Work Package 21 proposes the system-wide mechanisms through which we can strengthen the connection between mandate, resources, and results system-wide. while work package 18 proposes a funding architecture that increasingly finances and reports against the same results logic. Over time, the ambition is therefore quite practical. When member states give the United Nations a mandate, we should increasingly be capable of showing the strategic results we're pursuing, the capabilities and resources being applied, and the constraints we face and the results being achieved. And that in my, in our view is also the foundation for a more mature funding conversation. So where do we go from here? In my view, there's room for actions on both sides of the partnership. On the United Nations side, we need to strengthen system-wide results standards, improve transparency and communication, demonstrate more clearly what core funding enables. make pool funding more strategic and easier to understand, improve the quality and costing of earmarked funding, reduce unnecessary fragmentation, and create stronger management mechanisms for reviewing results and financing across the system. And if you're asking yourself how you could support, then there are equally important opportunities for member states to engage actively in the results and funding dialogues, to protect and strengthen core resources where possible, and to use pool funding where the collective action offers the greatest value, and to provide earmarked resources supporting strategy and discontinue low quality earmarking. To support full and transparent costing on both sides, managing institutional financial fragmentation, and to work with us in reducing that fragmentation alongside a more harmonized approach to reporting, visibility and accountability. Excellencies, before closing, let me just say the common objective of these two work packages is better mandate delivery. We want the United Nations that can see more clearly what is trying to achieve across the system, organizes capabilities around those results, finance those capabilities more strategically, and have a more facts-based and continuous dialogue with member states about performance, resources, and choices. That is the direction of travel we are putting forward. The proposals before you remain work in progress. The next stage is therefore important to develop them with member states, test what is useful, build mechanisms that strengthen both performance of the United Nations and the confidence of those who mandate and finance its work. With those words, thank you. And Mr. President, I'd like to hand back to you.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Group of 77 and China appreciates the overview provided by USG Guy Ryder, as well as the briefings on work packages 18, 21, and 22 by ASG Elizabeth Spehar and Special Advisor Jens Wandel. The Group welcomes the circulation of the pre-briefing materials and reiterates the importance of receiving documentation sufficiently in advance to enable substantive and informed engagement. The Group reaffirms its support for the objective of the UNIT initiative, strengthening the ability of the United Nations to deliver effectively and achieve greater impact on the ground. The process must remain transparent, inclusive and intergovernmental and fully respect mandates approved by Member States. Reform efforts should neither dilute mandates nor weaken the organisation's presence in programme countries. The Group emphasises that reforms identified as requiring intergovernmental consideration must not be implemented before such consideration has substantively taken place. The Secretariat must apply this principle consistently. Regarding work package 18, the group takes note of proposals aimed at improving the coherence and sustainability of the voluntary funding architecture. We recognize the complementary roles of core, pooled and earmarked resources. Nevertheless, predictable and sustainable voluntary funding, particularly core funding, remains indispensable. Any review of the UN funding architecture must not come at the expense of developing countries. The group would welcome additional clarification on positioning pool funding strategically, the proposed repositioning of the joint SDG fund, the development of system-wide results standards, and how these initiatives will take into account the diversity of mandates and operational context across the United Nations system. Concerning work package 21, the group acknowledges the value of strengthening the connection between mandates, resources and results across the United Nations system. A system-wide management for results, MFR mechanism, should build on existing reporting, avoid duplication and the creation of additional administrative layers and respect the mandates and governance arrangements of individual entities. Regarding the proposed mechanism of dialogue between UN system principles and Member States, the group underscores the importance of ensuring that this engagement is meaningful, transparent and inclusive, with the Secretariat playing a neutral role throughout the process. On actions 49, 55 and 58 in work package 22, the group takes note of the efforts to enhance coherence in prevention, peacebuilding and peace support, particularly in response to nationally identified priorities. Nonetheless, the group stresses that this exercise and the broader discussions on the regional reset and expertise on demand initiatives constitute two distinct conversations. reaffirmed that operational activities for development must remain firmly focused on poverty eradication in all its forms and dimensions as the overarching objective of the United Nations development system. Moreover, the group further underscores that the primary purpose of the resident coordinator system is to support sustainable development in programme countries. The system should therefore avoid mandate overlap, duplication and unnecessary reporting burdens, while ensuring that development functions are not diverted from their core objectives and that an effective and robust country presence is maintained. More broadly, the group underscores the need for greater clarity regarding the way forward, including the sequencing, timelines and intergovernmental consideration of proposals requiring Member State decisions. The group looks forward to receiving the outstanding information and reports sufficiently in advance and to continued engagement aimed at identifying realistic priorities, safeguarding the prerogatives of relevant governing bodies and ensuring transparent, inclusive and well-informed consultations. The group remains committed to engaging constructively in the UN process to advance a more effective, efficient, equitable and representative United Nations that strengthens mandate delivery. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uruguay. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Solomon Islands, speaking on behalf of Pacific Island Forum.

Thank you, Your Excellency. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the members of the Pacific Island Forum represented in New York. I thank the Under Secretary General and his team for today's briefing. On the UNAT review for funding mechanisms, we support a UN funding architecture that is sustainable, predictable, and coherent. We support proposals that advance meaningful funding reform and strengthen the UN's ability to deliver as a single system. resident coordinator system has the potential to play a critical role in strengthening the UN funding architecture through convincing partners, directing resources towards priorities identified in the cooperation frameworks and strengthening accountability. This requires stronger incentives of UN entities to work through the RCs, including through changes to accountability, reporting and funding structures. We also need to ensure RCs have the right skills, tools, experience, knowledge and seniority to be effective. We call on all Member States to meet the target set out in the funding compact. The compact is a key component in making the funding system more sustainable and coherent. Without these linkages, what we negotiate in New York has little impact on the ground where it actually matters at country level. Strengthening system-wide results management should not mean increased reporting burdens, practical, streamlined, managed, for result frameworks are needed and should be developed. In this regard, we approach the end of the 80th session of the General Assembly, PIF members would be grateful for an update on the process for forthcoming reports under work stream three, including how decisions will progress through the General Assembly. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Solomon Islands. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia on behalf of Cairns.

Thank you, President. I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of Canada. New Zealand and my own country Australia. CANSW thanks the briefers for their presentations. Today we'd like to make three points. First, on work package 18, CANSW welcomes the Secretary General's review of funding mechanisms and encourages the implementation of recommendations. At a time of fiscal constraint, it is more important than ever that all UN entities demonstrate better value for money, enhance transparency, achieve tangible results on the ground and operate as one UN. Implementing the recommendations can reduce fragmentation and transaction costs, improve transparency and accountability, and promote system-wide coherence. We see particular value in recommendation seven, better demonstrating the distinct value of core funding and what it enables compared to other modalities to increase donor confidence. And recommendation ten, strengthening country level funding compact dialogues to drive more progress against funding compact commitments. This should include resident coordinators as managers of cooperation frameworks being empowered to convene partners, direct resources towards agreed priorities, and strengthen accountability for system-wide results. Member states must also play their part. This includes advancing meaningful funding reforms, such as the proposals discussed in the operational activities for development segment through forthcoming intergovernmental processes, including the second committee. and paying their assessed contributions in full and on time in accordance with our obligations under the Charter. Second, on work package 21, CANS welcomes the Secretary-General's development of a management for results mechanism to strengthen how the UN's outcomes are measured and communicated. This work builds on Member States' requests of the Secretary-General in OP19 of resolution 80/251, mandate creation, implementation and review for an efficient and effective UN. This work package can provide member states with a clearer picture of the UN's collective results and limitations and improve senior leadership's ability to steer the UN system collectively. Third, on work package 22, CAN supports the Secretary General's efforts to build more coordinated, agile, and field orientated prevention, peacebuilding, and peace support. The new unified peacebuilding and peace support office will help provide more coordinated assistance to member states, supporting lasting peace, stronger institutions, and development. We welcome the focus on making the UN's prevention and peacebuilding capacities easier to identify, coordinate, and deploy. However, as prevention is truly a system-wide priority, we encourage the UN to think beyond the traditional peace and security architecture. Many of the risks that drive instability are addressed through development, humanitarian, governance, human rights, climate and economic interventions. In this regard, we support hosting regional peace and development advisers and regional commissions, integrating peace and development support in resident coordinator offices, and aligning surge capacities. This more integrated approach could leverage complementarity expertise to better deliver system-wide outcomes on the ground. We would welcome more information on how this will be funded. We also welcome the emphasis on support to nationally owned prevention strategies and peace finance. In our view, these provide a useful organising framework for bringing together the UN's political, development and financial tools around a common set of national priorities, and for strengthening partnerships with international financial institutions and regional development banks. Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, I deliver this statement on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Georgia, as well as Andorra, align themselves with this statement. We thank the briefers for the overview on the three work packages at hand. The EU is encouraged by the steps taken by the Secretariat to build a principled, more effective, cost efficient, and responsive United Nations. First, on work package 21, system-wide results management, the EU fully supports efforts to harmonize how impact is measured and communicated across the UN system. A consolidated and system-wide results management framework is central to fostering a culture of continuous improvement and to enhance strategic coordination and coherence. The design of this new framework should be as concrete as possible. This is crucial to strengthening trust among Member States and donors who must see UN funds being used efficiently, transparently and effectively. We reiterate, as we have in the ad hoc working group of workstream two, that Member States cannot review mandates and their implementation effectively without access to clear and evidence-based data from the Secretariat. We suggest that the Secretariat considers best practices from other international organizations which have recently successfully adopted new methodologies to assess their work. The EU appreciates the idea to introduce performance dialogues and would like to hear more on their budgetary implications. On work package 18, funding mechanisms, we must shift the balance towards more predictable, flexible and quality funding that allows the UN development system to act as one, not a collection of competing agencies. The funding compact was a step in the right direction, yet its implementation remains uneven. While ensuring that agencies, funds and programs can deliver on their mandates, resident coordinators must have the authority and resources to lead integrated development plans, contributing to an efficient and effective UN at the country level focused on delivering on the SDGs. We are deeply concerned by the organization's ongoing liquidity constraints, which carry serious operational implications, including for the UN development system. We encourage the strengthening of the joint SDG fund as the principal UN financing instrument for catalytic SDG action. As the largest donor to the UNDS, the EU and its member states call on all UN member states to pay their obligatory financial contributions in full and on time. Finally, on work package 22, prevention, peacebuilding and peace support, we welcome the progress identified by PBPSO and acknowledge the office's added value in supporting UN mission transitions, institution building for sustaining peace, supporting national prevention and peacebuilding strategies and peace finance. We call on PBPSO to continue coordinating the mapping of secretariat capacities. In this regard, we underline the essential role of peace and development advisors in providing cross-pillar prevention peacebuilding support at country and regional level and stress the need for their predictable and sustainable resourcing. Our key focus now is the implementation of the PVAR. One critical lesson from the review is the urgent need to communicate more effectively about the positive impact of peacebuilding. To support implementation, we have launched a year-long series of EU-supported events that will produce cross-regionally anchored policy recommendations on UN peacebuilding and conflict prevention by early next year. Colleagues, as we near the end of the GA's 80th session and the mandate of the Secretary General, we must continue to push for progress and ensure continuity and coordination across UN 80 tracks. On peace and security, the EU looks forward to the comprehensive review of the future of UN peace operations. On development, the ECOSOC resolution mentioned earlier on operational activities paves the way for reform that brings about a more coordinated UN that acts as one. In the humanitarian field, the first efforts to consolidate shared services have shown that resources can be optimized to enhance the UN's on-the-ground delivery. In the coming months, let us not lose sight of who this reform is for and of our ultimate end goal, a more agile and accountable UN that delivers across all three pillars and makes the world safer and more prosperous for all. Thank you very much.

A consolidated vision of contributions and collective results would strengthen the strategic steering capacity of the Secretary-General General and Secretariat Chiefs are providing Member States with a more unified view of how mandates are being implemented. My delegation welcomes the The guidelines that announced, which are light, adaptable, the lack of a new reporting level. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Ethiopia aligns itself with the statement delivered by Ruggie on behalf of the group of seven seven and China. While these contributions remain important, they are often supply-driven and may not always align with the priorities and mandates collectively agreed upon by member states. Demand-driven voluntary resources that directly support mandates approved by the relevant intergovernmental bodies are more effective and reflect the collective decision of member states. In this context, we strongly support recommendation five, which calls for greater discipline in the acceptance of earmarked funding. Such measures are the right steps toward enhancing strategic allocation of resources and clearly linking resources with mandates and results at system level. In conclusion, my delegation reiterates its support for the ongoing reform efforts and we remain committed for constructive engagement. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ethiopia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, President, and thank you to the briefers for their updates. Will they provide feedback, shape priorities, or drive change? And finally, on funding mechanisms, we welcome the strong progress and we support efforts to optimize the funding mix, ensuring each modality plays its most effective role. We particularly agree with recommendation five and the need for stronger discipline from agencies in accepting earmarked funding, focusing on accepting funds where they are best placed to deliver. Donors also have a role to play and we should assess approaches to earmarking as work on funding modalities continues. We welcome efforts to better demonstrate the value of core funding and particularly commend UNICEF's work in this area. We also support strengthened country-level funding dialogues led by the Resident Coordinator. Finally, President, we are committed to working together to achieve a more efficient, effective and impactful UN. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, President. Pakistan appreciates the briefings and the updates. And we welcome the clarifications provided by USG Ryder in this regard. On work package 22, Pakistan aligns with the observations made by the G77 and China on actions 49, 55 and 58. We have reservations regarding the proposed common portfolio framework spanning humanitarian development and peace building funds and would appreciate additional information on this proposal. and its practical implications. We also seek clarity on what substantive change is being proposed for the joint SDG fund beyond its redesignation. We do support recommendations four, five, six, and seven in this work package on earmarked contributions and better demonstrating what core funding delivers. On system-wide results management, we are open to mechanism that gives member states a clearer unified picture of results across the system provided it remains light, avoids new reporting burdens, and does not duplicate existing entity level accountability.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Pakistan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

Mr. President, France aligns itself with the statement made by the European Union. We would like to add the following in our national capacity. We would like to thank you firstly, Mr Under-Secretary-General, and all of the briefers today for giving us a clear overview of UNAT. President, with regard to programmes 18 and 21, France believes that these are closely interlinked and that a better harmonised measure of this could allow us to better guide our funding tomorrow. Mr President, Under Secretary General, looking at structural savings on salaries, purchasing costs, review of peace building and peacekeeping, the review and a more flexible development system are all important milestones that we will fully support. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of France. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia, followed by Suriname and then Brazil.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Mr. President. And the EU spoke on our behalf earlier, but I wanted to say, to put a few specific questions on package 22. And I thank the briefers. I appreciate the briefing and update on the UNAT as well as on implementation of Pact for the Future and the PBAR resolutions because in both of them prevention of conflicts featured quite prominently. And we appreciate the work, the progress that was done so far. Ajij Pejhar mentioned, and we agree with her, that the conflict prevention, sustaining peace and peace building is the core of what the UN is doing or should be doing. If nothing else, the chapter starts with to save future generations from the scourge of war, and we are not doing very well, are we, with a number of conflicts and collapsing world order. So to no surprise, I think in the past year discussions among the member states have been about returning to the origin, back to the basics, which is peace and security, including development and human rights as integral part of peace. And that's why also all six candidates for the Secretary General that we had the chance to meet and question put this topic as the prime topic. They were all talking about peace and security. They were all talking about bringing the UN back into the room, back behind the table, boots on the ground, or whatever language they used, but just to demonstrate that they are committed and this will be their focus. Of course, there are different candidates, but I think they speak the same language on this one, on prevention of conflicts, of peace building, of maintaining peace, on resilience for peace. And whoever will be appointed in the end by the General Assembly, this will be the focus of the UN. So yeah, to the question. And I know from facilitation of PBAR that PBSO was very ambitious. So question is whether the reconfiguration that was done in the merger is fit for the purpose of the needs of the UN in this field. And can this structure support the ambitious Secretary General in prevention of conflict, in mediation, in building peace? And also here, what is the relationship between PB, PSO, and mediation support unit. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia. I now give the floor to distinguished representative of Suriname, followed by Brazil and Switzerland.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Suriname aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. Suriname thanks Under-Secretary-General the Assistant Secretary General and the Special Advisor for the informative presentations on work packages 18, 21 and 22. UNAMI supports the objectives of the United Nation Aid Initiative and recognizes the importance of strengthening the United Nations so that it remains effective, responsive and fit for purpose. We appreciate the continued engagement of member states throughout this process. With respect to work package 18 on funding mechanisms, UNAM supports efforts to make core and pooled funding more predictable, coherent and effective. For developing countries, particularly small states, predictable and flexible funding is essential to enable the United Nations development system to respond to national priorities rather than fragmented funding streams. Reforms should therefore strengthen multilateral financing while preserving equitable access to all program countries. Regarding work package 21 on system-wide results management, we welcome efforts to improve coherence and harmonize reporting across the United Nations system. At the same time, any new framework should reduce, not increase, the reporting burden on program countries and UN country teams. Better management of results should ultimately translate into better delivery at the country level and greater accountability to member states. On work package 22 concerning prevention, peacebuilding, and peace support, Suriname strongly supports the emphasis of prevention. Investing in prevention, institution building, and nationally owned solution is both more effective and more cost efficient than responding after crisis have escalated. We also stress that peace building efforts should remain closely linked with sustainable development, climate resilience, and implementation of the 2030 agenda, particularly the vulnerable and small developing states. Finally, as discussion continues here, I underscore that reforms should preserve the universal character of the United Nations, be guided by the priorities of member states, and ensure that efficiency gains do not come at the expense of mandates or support to developing countries. We look forward to continuing our constructive engagement on the United Nations 80 initiative. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Suriname. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil, followed by Switzerland and Mexico.

Thank you, Mr. President. My delegation associates itself with the statement by the EU 77 and I join others in thanking the briefers and especially Mr. Ryder for continuously updating the General Assembly on the developments of the reform. A lot has been said, I share much of what has been said, so I'll be brief. Thank you.
I thank the Special Representative of Brazil, the distinguished representative of Brazil. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland, followed by Mexico and Timor-Leste.

Mr President, we would like to thank the various briefers for telling us about the most recent developments in the UNHCR initiative. Allow me to address the following points. Firstly, on prevention, peacebuilding and peace support, work package 22. Switzerland supports this more coherent, integrated approach focused on national needs for prevention and peacebuilding. The new structure should provide true added value, avoid duplication and ensure effective support on the ground, while also helping to strengthen collaborative approaches with humanitarian workers and development and to preserve the central role of the Resident Coordinator. On work package 18, funding mechanisms, Switzerland welcomes the efforts to optimize the implementation of mandates. in the current funding structure, while continuing to underscore the importance of increasing quality funding. In this regard, we support measures aimed at making core funding and pooled funding more attractive through better results reporting and communication about the basic compact, such as recommendations seven and eight. Regarding the joint financing, we support recommendations one and two, which aim to support joint funds and their governance to ensure the coherent architecture of We propose that lessons learned from the humanitarian, uh, wing be fully integrated. We support recommendation nine, strengthening oversight and accountability in funding thanks to an annual high level review of the funding compact. We also believe that strengthening the role of governing, uh, executive boards. will help contribute to these objectives. We support measures aimed at ensuring that funding is strictly earmarked funding be correctly aligned in accordance with recommendations five and six. A differentiated cost recovery based on the quality of funding is a key element in this regard. As a contributor, Switzerland welcomes efforts to provide additional impetus to the Fund. We would be grateful, however, to have clarifications about the expected impact of this repositioning, particularly when it comes to funding and future options. Lastly, when it comes to system-wide results management, Work Package 21, Switzerland welcomes the efforts made in the context of this work package to strengthen results-based management at the system-wide level. We believe that improving the link between mandates, resources and results is essential to continue promoting an approach that is more results focused within the United Nations system. Switzerland encourages efforts that are based on existing mechanisms and frameworks and avoids useless duplication. The added value of this mechanism should lie in strengthening coherence, transparency and a better understanding of system wide results. Switzerland reaffirms its commitment to participating constructively in the UN reform process, the UNAT reform process. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland. I now call on -- I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico, followed by Timor-Leste and Republic of Korea.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. We thank the briefers for their presentations. My country attaches vital importance to this exercise. with the growing budgetary pressures and as one of the top 20 contributors to the United Nations, it is essential for us that we correct the asymmetries that are affecting the organization and give it back the role that it needs to play in prevention, peacebuilding and peacekeeping. Therefore, it's necessary to make progress on various different fronts to achieve a more efficient financing architecture, more robust and harmonized accountability mechanisms and greater consistency between mandates and structures on the ground. The Work packages 18, 21 and 22 analyse these dimensions in a complementary way in order to achieve institutional strengthening. Faced with the increase in interstate armed conflicts, the legitimacy of the UN in the face of international public opinion will depend on its ability to prevent crises, to mediate with credibility and to re-establish the minimum conditions for peace. Mexico takes note of the tangible progress made in work package 22 and we thank Ms Speja for the information that she has provided regarding the new PBPSO that begins in January. We hope that this will continue to lead to political support and a greater impact and transparency effort for the membership and we would welcome regular updates about the progress of that reconfiguration. We in particular value the identification of financial fragmentation, the differentiated donor requirements and inconsistencies in cost recovery. In that regard, it is important to make progress towards a balance that strengthens financial flexibility without undermining the ability of Member States to focus their contributions in line with their priorities. We would like to focus efforts also on three specific points. Firstly, providing political support to the Secretary General so that he can appoint special representatives and envoys with experience in mediation, political sensitivity and the capacity to engage in dialogue. Second, to ensure predictable financing for the regular budget for good offices, prevention and mediation and integrated planning from the Executive Office of the SG, DPPA and DPO and the country teams. And the goal for us is to link early warning with early response. We would also like to prioritise light and rapid deployment mechanisms to support ceasefires and ensure humanitarian access when a traditional mission is not in place. Mexico will always support a reform that allows for a continued effect on the ground and to win back the trust of populations in this organization and its member states. Thank you very much.
Thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste, followed by Republic of Korea and the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, Timor-Leste thanks briefers for the valuable insights. We align ourselves with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of G77 and China. Mr. President, we welcome the proposal and funding mechanisms, which stands liquidity constraints continue to affect the organization's ability to implement and mandates effectively. This is particularly important for countries with limited administrative capacity. Mr. President, as a country that benefited from sustainable and peaceful support, Timor-Leste understands that prevention is not only more effective but also more cost effective than responding to the crisis after they emerge. We therefore support effort to strengthen policy coherence and enhance the United Nations capacity to respond to nationally identified priorities through more coherent engagement across the peace, development, human rights, and humanitarian pillars as appropriate. Mr. President, taken together, these three work packages demonstrate that a stronger mandate delivery depends on current financing, effective result management and sustained investment and prevention. As these reforms advance, they should remain responsible to the needs and priorities of member states, particularly developing countries, including SEEDS and LDCs. Timor-Leste remain committed to engaging constructively in the UN active process

and look forward to continuing this dialogue.

I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea, followed by the Islamic Republic of Iran and China.

Thank you, President, for convening this meeting. I also thank all the secretariat briefers for the information shared. Allow me to add a few more comments and questions on work package 21 and work package 18. On management for results, MFR mechanism, we encourage efforts to strengthen and harmonize performance management frameworks across the UN system. We understand that the work is underway to develop a function within the mandate registry that would allow member states to view the linkages between mandates, resources, activities, and results. We would appreciate clarification as to whether this forms part of the broader effort to establish a system-wide MFR mechanism. It also has been indicated that the MFR mechanism would make use of existing reporting mechanisms and not create additional administrative burdens. On that basis, how will the dialogue between the leadership of the UN system and member states be structured? Finally, under the current plan, the MFR framework is to be developed progressively by the end of 2027. We request that the basic concept and implementation plan be developed at an early stage and submitted for consideration by member states so that the initiative can be implemented without delay. With regard to funding mechanisms, we would like to better understanding the specific implications that the 10 proposed recommendations may have for donor countries. and request detailed clarification on the following questions. First, could the Secretariat clarify what systematically considering pooled funding means and what a common portfolio framework across humanitarian development and peacebuilding fund is? Second, if the role of the joint SDG fund is strengthened, how might this affect the range of choices available to donor countries, including providing earmarked contributions directly to entities? Third, how is the assessment of the quality of earmarked contributions expected to affect the modalities through which member states provide funding? Fourth, would the annual review of the funding compact and country level dialogues create any new consultation obligations for donor countries? Last but not least, given that the discussions are at an early stage, my delegation requests that sufficient consultations be held with member states on this work package. In this regard, we would like to know how the Secretariat plans to consult with member states in progressing the suggested recommendations. Republic of Korea reiterates its appreciation on the role of the Secretariat for supporting member states by providing expertise, evidence, and information, and also guiding necessary discussions. We encourage you to continue to do so, and we will remain committed to engaging constructively in strengthening this organization's capacity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea. And I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran, followed by China and Egypt.

Thank you, Mr. President. Islamic Republic of Iran aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of Group of 77 and China. My delegation thanks USG Guy Ryder, ASG Elizabeth Sbar, and Special Adviser Jens Wandel for the briefings and for the information provided on work packages 18, 21, and 22. We appreciate continued efforts to engage member states throughout the UNAT process. We take note of the UNAT initiative's objective to enhance the effectiveness and impact of the United Nations. In this regard, reform efforts should build on existing intergovernmental processes and governance structures while ensuring meaningful, transparent and inclusive engagement with Member States at every stage. The Secretariat should continue to maintain a neutral role throughout this process. We also stressed the importance of avoiding parallel mechanisms, additional administrative layers and duplicative reporting requirements. Reform should simplify processes, improve efficiency and make better use of existing institutional capacities. On work package 18, my delegation emphasizes that the current financial challenges should be addressed by tackling the root causes. Nothing can substitute for the fundamental obligation of member states to pay their assessed contributions in full, on time and without conditions, while refraining from actions that impede other member states from meeting their financial obligations. Although the current funding mix is likely to persist, earmarked voluntary contributions should remain aligned with the UN mandates rather than drive programmatic priorities. Otherwise, they risk distorting organizational priorities, weakening strategic planning, and compromising the impartial implementation of mandates. Regarding work package 21, any new arrangement should remain results oriented, build on existing reporting frameworks and fully respect the mandates and governance structures of the individual entities. A stronger focus on measurable outcomes and impact on the ground should remain the guiding principle of reform. Finally, we look forward to greater clarity on the sequencing timelines and intergovernmental consideration of proposals requiring member decisions on

stream three.

Thank you so much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Iran. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China, followed by Egypt.

President, I thank you for convening today's meeting. I thank the briefers for their updates. China supports the statement made by Uruguay on behalf of G77 and China. The UN80 initiative is now in a critical phase that requires solid implementation with more granularity. We encourage the Secretariat to continue advancing the reforms in an inclusive and transparent manner, address the concerns of all parties, especially developing countries, and enhance the overall effectiveness of this organization. Development should be prioritized to help the countries eradicate poverty, tap development potential, and reinforce the economic and social foundation for lasting peace on the pooled funding mechanism. Efforts should be made to avoid duplication among the joint SDG fund, the central emergency response fund and the peacebuilding fund to prevent wasting resources and unnecessarily adding to the financial burdens on member states. Traditional donors should continue to bear the primary responsibility for funding. Regarding the system-wide management for results, the ultimate purpose of the mandate implementation review is to enhance quality and efficiency. China encourages the secretariat to strengthen internal coordination, strengthen relevant mechanisms, maintain a results-oriented approach, and ensure member states can track progress and assess outcomes in a timely manner. China remains committed to working with all parties to advance reforms in a direction that benefits the long-term development of the UN and serve the common interests of its member states. I thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair, for giving Egypt the floor. Allow me first to say that we align ourselves with the statement delivered by the Chair of the G77. Mr. Chair, we thank all the briefers for their sober presentations. A lot has been said in the previous interventions, so we'll focus ours on work package 22. Egypt appreciates the efforts undertaken under the UNAD initiative and its overall direction of strengthening prevention. peacebuilding and peace support through a more integrated and field-oriented approach. The emphasis on nationally led priorities, mission transitions, institution building and more coherent support across the peace continuum is fully consistent with the guidance recently provided by Member States through the 2025 peacebuilding architecture review. We also appreciate all the efforts performed in this regard by the PBPSO under the able leadership of AGS Bihar and believe that the recent structuring and expansion of the office mandate is a step on the right direction. In addition, also welcome the objective of further reducing the fragmentation by bringing together expertise on peace building, DDR, SSR and justice and corrections while improving search support to the field, which is if implemented well, will enhance the UN's ability to provide more timely and coherent support to countries emerging from conflict. Having said that, allow me, Mr. Chair, to ask a couple of questions that we appreciate further clarification on. First, through the presentations, the PBBSO was referred to as a center of excellence, a bridge and the hinge across the system, but it remains unclear, uh, regarding the decision making and the coordination, uh, uh, um, the the coordination dynamics in this regard with the relevant entities in the HQ and on the ground. We believe that the office should be empowered when it comes to peace building and prevention related activities. And that's why clear governance arrangements and success indicators will be essential to avoid any kind of duplication in this regard. Secondly, in relation to partnerships, we want to ask how will the comparative advantages of regional organizations such as the African Union will be reflected operationally under the current plan? to ensure the full utilization of subsidiarity when it comes to peacebuilding and conflict prevention efforts. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt. We have heard the last statement of our speakers today. I now give the floor to Madam Elizabeth Spehar, Assistant Secretary-General for Peacebuilding and Peace Support to give her comments or answer some of the questions raised.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair, and thank you so much to all here for a very rich set of comments and questions. I am very grateful for that. I have been taking furious notes to make sure that I could respond to as many of the comments and, in particular, the questions as possible. I hope that I will be able to go through all or most of them in the time allotted. First of all, there were a number of mentions of the peace and development advisers and the interests of a number of speakers in regional peace and development advisors, which the Secretary General has mentioned. I can say that I think it is universally understood that the PDAs, or peace and development advisors, who are managed jointly by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and UNDP, they are seen as extremely important tools on the ground. And There, of course, is a hope that there can be regional PDAs at some point. I do not directly manage that particular file, but my understanding is that the main impediment at the moment is financial, that there are not enough resources coming in at the moment also for regional PDAs. And in terms of the analysis of of the system, it was seen that the national level PDAs were the ones who seemed to add the best value at this point. But of course, this would be the aspiration, I believe, to be able to have also regional PDAs. As you may know, there is a mix of both international peace and development advisors as well as national peace and development advisors in a number of places. And I think that that's also very important in terms of what a number of you have mentioned with respect to institution building, capacity building, to also have national capacity in this area that can remain in the country through these national colleagues. I wanted to mention that in terms of, in my understanding where we are with PDAs at the moment, is that by the second-half of this year, the joint program between DPPA and UNDP that manages the PDAs will have a field capacity of 27 international PDAs, 24 national peace and development officers, two UNVs and nine secondees. So this is the level of capacity that we are able to deploy at the moment. Hopefully, more could be done with additional financing. I can also mention that, from where I sit in PBPSO, we have been working on some creative arrangements where we can perhaps save some resources by having a head of a PBF secretariat also play the role of PDA or actually the reverse, that a PDA could also provide that function and in that way we are saving money by having one individual instead of two. On the point on prevention going beyond the peace and security pillar that was mentioned by Australia on behalf of CANZ, if I remember correctly. Yes, absolutely. A number of you mentioned explicitly the peace, the humanitarian development and peace nexus. We feel that we have a number of tools and capacities that can contribute, based on Member State demand, towards both the preparation and implementation of national prevention strategies. The Peacebuilding Fund supported through funding various agencies, funds and programs were involved in support. But we also need to look towards the role of the international financial institutions and how they can support peacebuilding in fragile and conflict-affected contexts, the role of the private sector, so peace positive, as we like to call it, peace positive investment in countries, which could be domestic private sector or international private sector. So we are working to try to help build what we call a broader peace finance ecosystem to support member states with their prevention peacebuilding efforts. And again, we are one of the cogs in the wheel. We have some colleagues that have been concentrating quite a bit on this, but it's not us doing this alone in a silo. We are working across the system on this issue. In terms of support to mission transitions, which was also mentioned and which I mentioned in my presentation, again, we have been analyzing as a very new office what we can offer to be even more coherent and efficient in our support to the field, because that is, of course, the main The main aim is to support member states in their countries. And we realize that we do have a number of tools that we can bring together more cohesively. The financing through the Peacebuilding Fund, which has as one of its priorities support to UN mission transitions, the link with the IFIs, the SSR, DDR, justice and corrections tools. and so forth. But again, the point is that this would be done, and I hope increasingly coherently through our office, but in connection with the rest of the UN system. We are not the only tools, we are not the only office. The idea is that one of our value adds can be in the area of UN mission transitions, but clearly that has to be done with our appropriate colleagues across the peace and security pillar, as well as across the system more broadly, the agency's funds and programs have a critical role as well to play in UN mission transitions in terms of the follow-up and so forth. There was a mention also of the PBAR implementation, implementation of the peacebuilding architecture review, and the importance of looking at impact. As some of you may know, we've been trying very hard as an office to work more on being able to produce evidence and clear information on results, data-driven and so forth. And so in terms of the Peacebuilding Fund, we are working increasingly to do impact assessments, thematic reviews and other things that can help to show results and impact for the the resources expended. Similarly, we have the Peacebuilding Impact Hub, which is looking at peacebuilding impact, not just from our office or from PBF, but really across the system and beyond.
